Blind Artist Creates Ganesha & Shiva Idols by Touch

At eight years old Anjali began losing her sight, a process that progressed until doctors confirmed her eyes could no longer function. Treatments and an operation offered hope, but restoration proved impossible. Rather than accept a life without visual input, Anjali turned to her hands. As a child she crafted diyas and later clay toys, and visits to temples inspired her to shape idols of Ganesha, Shiva and other deities. She feels every curve, line and detail, converting tactile perception into sculpture. Despite early comments that blindness made her useless, she maintained the belief that any ability a "normal" person has is also within her reach. Supported by family and community, her clay idols are now displayed and admired. Her story, featured on The Better India, underscores how tactile skill can replace visual cues in artistic practice. Each finished figure becomes a testament to perseverance, encouraging others with disabilities to explore alternative pathways. Why it matters: talent thrives when limitations are reframed as opportunities.

Lost Both Arms at 11, Then Won Arjuna Award | Suyash Jadhav

Suyash Jadhav was told he would never swim again after a tragic accident at age 11 left him without both arms below the elbows. After nearly three years away from the water, he returned to swimming and never looked back. Jadhav went on to claim India’s first Asian Para Games swimming gold, compete at three Paralympic Games, accumulate more than 150 medals, and receive the prestigious Arjuna Award. His journey from an unfinished childhood dream to a record‑breaking career illustrates remarkable determination and resilience. Today, he stands as a role model for aspiring para athletes across the nation, showing that physical limits can be transcended through perseverance. Why it matters: his story expands possibilities for para athletes and underscores the power of resilience.
